newsitem.title: TAIWAN: INTERVIEW-PanAmSat feeds on open markets, high-tech.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-PanAmSat feeds on open markets, high-tech.

text.p: Satellite giant PanAmSat, beefed up by a merger with Hughes Communications' Galaxy network, says deregulation and high-tech innovation are creating global opportunities that were unimaginable five years ago.

"They say everything is timing," PanAmSat president and chief executive Fred Landman said from the firm's headquarters in Greenwich, Conn. "And you also need execution. We've been executing our plan," he said in a telephone interview.
Friday's merger with Galaxy demonstrates PanAmSat's strong sense of timing and execution -- and its business acumen.

Already the largest private network with four satellites in orbit, PanAmSat Corp will more than triple in size through its billion-dollar tie-up with Hughes' 10-orbiter Galaxy network. Seven more satellites will be launched in 1997-98.

The merger, which was announced in September and passed its final U.S. regulatory hurdle on April 17, creates a publicly held company called PanAmSat Corp with some US$700 million in combined annual sales.
Existing PanAmSat shareholders, who overwhelmingly approved the merger, will get US$1.5 billion in cash -- US$30 per share -- and 28.5 percent of the new company.
Hughes Electronics Corp, parent of space firm Hughes Communications and a subsidiary of U.S. carmaker General Motors Corp, will hold 71.5 percent of the new PanAmSat.

Landman called PanAmSat's finances sound, citing a recent ratings upgrade by Standard & Poor's and the deep pockets of its new corporate parents. He said PanAmSat had no imminent public financing plans despite its ambitious launch schedule.
Landman said the satellite business had changed dramatically over the past five years, reflecting major technological innovations as well as steady deregulation.

On the high-tech side, a switch to highly compressible digital television from analog, the growth of direct satellite television and soaring of demand for internet and other digital telecoms had sharply shifted PanAmSat's focus.
"Five years ago, direct TV was not any part of our business. Today it's over 20 percent of our business and going forward."
"Our job is to find where technology is moving, what's being developed and what people want to do to try to mesh these things together," Landman said.

PanAmSat has launched an internet carrier service that can beam internet into homes via small, low-cost rooftop antennae at 28 times the speed of a standard 14.4 kbps modem. The system is operating in Japan and the United States, he said.
On the regulatory side, liberalisation of many countries' broadcast and communications markets is spurring huge demand for satellites to carry direct and cable-based TV, he said.
In Taiwan, for example, satellites now deliver scores of new television channels that only a few years ago would have been illegal. Newcomer Formosa TV airs two channels over PanAmSat.
Landman said the World Trade Organisation's February telecom pact would drive the satellite business by ensuring that firms with global ambitions have the tools for global reach.
"What's going on with regulation and opening up markets, in addition to technology, is going to fuel growth," he said.
Landman said satellite is particularly attractive to less developed countries with poor terrestrial communications.
"Satellite are instant infrastructure," he said.
India has contracted to use PanAmSat to transmit dozens of TV channels directly to 65-cm (26 inch) rooftop dishes.
The merger with Galaxy means broadcasters can span the globe via one supplier. China Central Television has a deal to beam up to six digital TV channels worldwide using PanAmSat's network.
"Now I don't have to leave CCTV on the loading dock waiting to be picked up by another carrier," he said.
